items: Question and scope - one question (which supplier has the highest return rate, and what should we investigate next?), one period (2025-09 to 2026-08), four receiving sites, three suppliers, 144 delivery records, one definition: return rate is total units returned divided by total units shipped, the same scope for every comparison. The decision the deck supports is named on the title slide: is a supplier follow-up warranted?

The comparison - a bar chart with the numbers beside it: Bravo Plastics 262 returns / 75,184 shipped = 0.348%; Cardinal Metals 96 / 74,658 = 0.129%; Alpha Components 74 / 75,060 = 0.099%. A side note closes the obvious objection: shipment volumes are nearly equal, so the rate gap is not a volume artifact.

The trend - Bravo's monthly return rate across the twelve months: elevated and volatile, peaking at 0.737% in April 2026, quiet near 0.14% in June and July, back at 0.465% in August. The commentary says only what twelve points can support: no steady improvement - and no claim of seasonality or cause.

The proposed follow-up - a two-panel slide. Left, labeled findings: the rate gap, its persistence, and the separate fact that Bravo drives 1,157 of the 2,207 inspection defect occurrences. Right, labeled judgment: ask Bravo for a returns root-cause review, pull the records behind the highest-return months, agree a target and re-measure next quarter on the same definition.

Limitations and next steps - descriptive, not causal; no delivery counts exist, so no overall delivery rate is claimed anywhere; one inspection-hours value is missing (missing, not zero); inspection defects and customer returns are two measures that are never added together. Then the single decision requested: approve the review.

blocks.text: The separation rule

Findings are what the workbook supports; recommendations are labeled proposals. The mock deck makes the boundary physical - two panels, two headings - because that separation is the trust move that survives every audience question. It matters most exactly where the story gets tempting. The verified scorecard carries units-weighted unit costs: Alpha Components $12.4299, Bravo Plastics $9.9030, Cardinal Metals $14.1804. The tension is real - the cheapest supplier is also the most-returned - and it is precisely where a weak deck starts inventing: a projected savings figure, a quality-cost trade-off, a committed benefit. The mock deck states no cost claim anywhere, because the data cannot support one; what switching or fixing would cost is a question for the proposed review, not for this dataset.

blocks.title: The invented benefit
blocks.body: The prompt forbids invented causes and unsupported benefits for a reason: a decision audience remembers the number you made up, not the caveat you attached to it. Bravo's low unit cost ($9.9030 against $12.4299 and $14.1804) invites a savings story the workbook cannot back - leave it out.

blocks.text: Check it like an artifact

items: Coverage: count five slides and map each one to the coverage list in the prompt.
Fidelity: reconcile every displayed number to the analysis - at minimum trace the 0.348% comparison and the April 2026 peak of 0.737% back to the workbook.
Narrative: read only the slide titles. Do they tell the story alone, from question to evidence to proposal to limits?
Delivery: open the exported file and inspect it - no clipped text, readable at projection size, speaker notes present on every slide, charts still editable.

blocks.title: Not decorated bullet points
blocks.body: A presentation is an artifact with narrative, fidelity, and delivery requirements. One main message per slide, every number traced to the source, and the limitations named out loud are what let the deck survive its first hard question.

blocks.title: Audit before reuse
blocks.body: Run the four checks on Supplier_Quality_Mock_Presentation.pptx before you reuse the prompt on your own analysis. The sample is deliberately auditable - the limitations slide names what the data cannot say, which is the habit to copy.

sections.heading: Step 6: organize the email thread

blocks.text: An email summary has a job to do. A long thread read top to bottom is a chronology, and a chronological retelling can obscure the current decision - the thing the person asking for the summary actually needs. Before writing any prompt, decide what the summary must answer. Four questions cover most jobs: the current situation (what is true now?), decisions (what was agreed, and under what conditions?), actions (who owes what, by when?), and open questions (what still needs an answer?). The same source thread can support a current-state brief, an action table, or preparation for your reply - the job determines the shape.
Choose the result you need

One thread can serve five different jobs, and choosing the job IS the prompt - one sentence each once the outcome is named. In Outlook the workflow is: run the built-in Copilot summary first, then refine it in the Copilot chat pane, scoped to the same conversation, with the line that matches what you need.

rows: "Summarize the current situation in three sentences."
"List changed dates or decisions and show the latest version."
"Create a table with task, owner, due date, and dependency."
"List unanswered questions, approval conditions, and missing attachments."
"Draft a concise response. Use brackets where I still need to decide. Do not invent commitments."

blocks.text: The five output shapes, named
Behind the menu sit five reusable output shapes. Naming the shape is what turns "summarize this" into a specification - each shape has a job, and blank cells beat guessed ones in every one of them.

cols: What it is - and when to use it
rows: One sentence, ~30 words: current state or decision needed - not the history. For clearing an inbox.
OVERVIEW · DECISIONS · ACTION ITEMS · OPEN QUESTIONS. The default when filing, forwarding, or catching up - the prompt below is this shape, grown up.
Task | Owner | Due | Blocked by. For moving work into your to-do system.
Decision | Decided by | Reasoning | Date - settled items only, proposals flagged. For defending choices later.
Every unanswered question + “X owes Y: [thing]”, latest state only. For preparing your reply.

blocks.text: The requirement types for this artifact: source scope, current state, decisions and conditions, actions and ownership, date meaning, evidence traceability, attachments, and the authority boundary. Chronology and evidence dominate: a useful summary preserves who said what and when, keeps every condition attached to its approval, and traces each claim to a supporting message. The email-summaries table in references/Requirements_by_Artifact.md pairs each type with its acceptance check.

Review this thread using only the messages and attachments you can access. Give me the current status, confirmed decisions and conditions, action items with owner and due date, changed dates or commitments, unanswered questions, missing attachments, and messages that need a reply. Write ‘Not stated’ when the thread does not say. Cite the supporting message by sender and date.
blocks.caption: The structured brief, verbatim - workbook tab 4-Summarize-Email.

blocks.text: Notice the honesty machinery. "Not stated" beats a guessed owner or date. Superseded dates are marked as superseded instead of silently replaced. Source facts are separated from interpretation. The prompt ends by asking for the next clarification needed - a summary that surfaces what to ask is worth more than one that papers over it. And the last sentence is an authority boundary: a reply, if requested, is a draft for human review; nothing is sent.
The practice thread

The practice material is a fictional packaging-change conversation: ten messages, six people, supplied as Packaging_Change_Thread.txt in references/exercise-data/ so you can paste it into any approved assistant. The attachment mentioned in message 5 is intentionally not supplied.

rows: Target the packaging change for Sep 25; Luis to confirm the trial plan.
Can run the trial on Sep 18, subject to quality review.
Approved provided total trial cost stays within 18,000 and quality signs off.
The drawing mentioned in the plan must be sent before he can approve the trial.
Says the drawing is attached; material shipment arrives Sep 23.
Sep 25 not feasible; proposed change date is now Oct 2; Luis to update the trial plan by Sep 16.
Who pays the extra freight for the later shipment?
Will submit the trial plan by Sep 16; the trial date is now Sep 25.
The 18,000 cap still applies; additional freight charges not approved.
Plan for Oct 2, pending Ben's sign-off; Luis owns the plan; freight decision still needed.
blocks.note: Fictional training material; the full text is also reproduced in the course deck's reference appendix.

blocks.text: The four traps
The thread is engineered so that a naive "summarize this" fails in observable ways. Four traps are planted, and a good brief catches all of them.

rows: The change date is Oct 2, superseding Sep 25. The trial date is Sep 25, superseding Sep 18. Two different dates changed - do not conflate them.
Approved within the 18,000 cap and pending quality sign-off. A bare "approved" is wrong, and freight extras are explicitly not approved.
Freight responsibility was raised and stays unresolved - an open question with no invented owner or resolution.
The drawing is referenced but not accessible. Its content must not be summarized, and quality sign-off waits on it.

blocks.text: The open items complete the picture: Luis's trial plan is committed and due September 16; Ben's sign-off is open with no stated due date - write "Not stated" rather than inventing one; the freight decision has no owner; the material arrives September 23. Note the decision statuses too: the October 2 change is planned, not finally approved, because it still waits on quality sign-off - which in turn waits on the drawing nobody can open. The expected brief lives in the workbook's instructor tab KEY-Email and in references/exercise-data/instructor-keys/Packaging_Change_Expected_Brief.md.

blocks.title: Success check
blocks.body: Your brief catches the moved change date (Oct 2, conditional on sign-off), the trial date (Sep 25 superseding Sep 18), the 18,000 cap with freight not approved, and the missing drawing - and it gives Ben no invented due date.

blocks.title: Facts, then open questions
blocks.body: Email work begins by separating known facts from unanswered questions. The latest state supersedes earlier dates, but an unanswered question stays open - a summary that quietly resolves it has invented a decision.

blocks.text: Where to run it

The pasted-text path is the primary one: paste Packaging_Change_Thread.txt and the prompt into any approved assistant. It always works and needs no particular license. There is also a native path, verified as of September 2026: Microsoft Outlook offers "Summary by Copilot" on an open thread, with numbered citations that click through to the source message - the citations are your verification tool - and any drafted reply stays a draft. The full experience depends on your organization's Copilot license, which is exactly why the supplied-text version is the one this course drills. Either way, the prompt above is a portable specification: scope, extraction fields, evidence rules, and authority boundaries travel with you across tools.

Draft my reply for review: answer what the thread can answer, confirm decisions WITH their conditions, and propose one next step per unresolved item. Leave [brackets] where I must decide. Do not send anything.
blocks.caption: The optional follow-up - a draft is the boundary; sending stays human.

blocks.title: Practice on fiction only
blocks.body: Never practice on real confidential threads. The packaging conversation exists so you can drill extraction on material that is safe to paste anywhere; run your first summaries on it, not on live mail.

sections.heading: Step 7: extract the quotes

blocks.text: After the email arc the case turns commercial. Three fictional quotation documents - Quote_Alpha_Components.pdf, Quote_Bravo_Plastics.pdf, and Quote_Cardinal_Metals.pdf in references/exercise-data/ - answer the follow-up the analysis proposed. The job is documents in, spreadsheet out, and it is deliberately split into two steps: faithful extraction first, judgment second.

Review the attached supplier quotation files and create an editable Excel workbook.

Create a Raw Extraction sheet with one row per quotation and these fields: supplier, quoted scope, currency, quoted quantity, unit price, tooling or other one-time charges, freight, taxes, lead time, payment terms, quote validity, exclusions, source file, source page, and missing information.

Copy values exactly as stated. Keep currencies, quantities, and units in their original form. Write ‘Not stated’ when a field is absent. Do not normalize, rank, or recommend yet. Cite the source file and page for every extracted commercial value.
blocks.caption: The extraction prompt, verbatim - workbook tab Quote-Extract.

blocks.text: Every discipline in that prompt exists because its absence has a failure mode. Verbatim values, because a "helpfully" rounded price cannot be audited. Original currencies and units, because silent conversion smuggles in an unstated exchange rate. "Not stated" for absent fields, because a guessed freight term looks exactly like a real one. And a source file and page per commercial value, so any number can be checked against its document in seconds.

blocks.title: Extraction before judgment
blocks.body: Mixing extraction with comparison is how errors hide: a wrong number that enters the sheet unnoticed poisons every later calculation. Step 7 produces a sheet you can verify against the source documents; only then does step 8 get to reason on it.

blocks.text: The prepared example ships as references/exercise-data/Quote_Comparison_Workbook.xlsx (sheet "Raw Extraction"), and the instructor key as instructor-keys/Quote_Comparison_Key.md - grade your run against the documents first, the key second.

sections.heading: Step 8: compare the quotes - and refuse to pick a winner

blocks.text: Comparison is where invented certainty creeps in, so the prompt makes the rule explicit: normalize only what has a stated basis, show the formulas, and keep the original values visible next to every derived one.

Using the Raw Extraction sheet, create a Normalized Comparison sheet.

Normalize quantities, units, or currencies only when the conversion rule or basis is supplied. Keep every original extracted value visible. Flag differences in scope, assumptions, exclusions, and commercial terms. Show formulas for comparable totals.

Do not identify a best quote until the comparison basis is complete. List the missing information and unresolved questions that prevent a fair recommendation.
blocks.caption: The comparison prompt, verbatim - workbook tab Quote-Compare.

blocks.text: Run on the three sample documents, the arithmetic itself is easy. At the quoted 5,000-unit volume with one-time tooling spread across the units, Alpha Components lands at USD 15.60 per unit (13.90 plus 8,500 of tooling over 5,000 units) on FOB terms; Bravo Plastics at EUR 14.70 per unit (11.90 plus a 2.80 charge) EXW; Cardinal Metals at USD 16.40 all-in, DDP, tooling waived. And that is exactly where a careful comparison stops: Bravo is quoted in euros with no exchange-rate basis supplied, and the three delivery terms put freight, duties, and risk on different sides of the line.

blocks.title: The correct answer is "not yet"
blocks.body: The sample quotes are engineered so the honest deliverable is a comparison that stops - naming the euro conversion basis, freight, and taxes as blocking gaps - rather than a winner. If your run picked a best quote, it invented at least one basis; find which.

blocks.text: A defensible "cannot compare yet, and here is exactly what is missing" is a better deliverable than a confident wrong recommendation - it hands the requester a short list of questions instead of a decision built on air. The prepared sheet ("Normalized Comparison" in the same workbook) and the instructor key show the full expected shape.

sections.heading: Step 9: reference files become a research workbook

blocks.text: The last live step generalizes everything the quotes taught. The material is a research pack - references/exercise-data/research-pack/, four fictional files: a quality-manual excerpt, a supplier-quality newsletter, an undated scorecard guideline, and an 8D problem-solving one-pager - and a research question: how should supplier quality reviews be run? The deliverable is a workbook in three sheets: Evidence, Synthesis, Sources.

Review the attached reference files and build a research workbook using only information you can trace to a source.

Create an Evidence sheet with one claim, instruction, or finding per row and these columns: ID, topic, claim or instruction, source file, author or organization, date, page or section, short supporting excerpt, plain-language interpretation, caveat or limitation, relevance to [research question], confidence or status, and open question.

Create a Synthesis sheet that orders the findings from foundations to implications and identifies agreements, conflicts, and gaps.

Create a Sources sheet that indexes every file.

Write ‘Not stated’ when information is missing. Keep conflicting claims separate. Do not invent citations. Add filters, freeze the header row, and wrap long text. Deliver an editable Excel workbook. If the tool cannot create an Excel file, provide separate comma-separated values (CSV) tables.
blocks.caption: The research prompt, verbatim - workbook tab Research.

blocks.text: The pack is engineered the way real source material behaves: two of the sources disagree on review cadence - the manual excerpt says quarterly, the newsletter says monthly - and the scorecard guideline carries no date at all.

blocks.title: Conflicts stay visible
blocks.body: The Evidence sheet must carry both cadence claims as separate rows, the Synthesis sheet must name the conflict as a conflict, and the undated guideline keeps "Not stated" in its date column. A tidy synthesis that quietly picks a side is a defect - however confident it reads.

blocks.text: The prepared example ships as references/exercise-data/Research_Workbook.xlsx - twelve traced evidence rows, a synthesis that names the agreements, the conflict, and the gaps, and a source index - with the instructor key in instructor-keys/Research_Workbook_Key.md.

sections.heading: Reference exercise: explain a topic clearly

blocks.text: One artifact steps out of the live hour in this edition and into the reference layer: the plain-language document. It remains part of the method - run it as self-study, with the same requirement discipline as everything above.

The fifth artifact is a plain-language document, and it corrects a common misunderstanding: explaining something simply is a requirements problem - audience, vocabulary, fidelity, and a learning check - not dumbing down. The dominant risk is not that the text stays too hard; it is that the simplification quietly changes the meaning. A dropped condition, an analogy stretched past where it holds, a caveat that vanished - each reads smoothly and misleads reliably.

The requirement types: reader and purpose, vocabulary, structure, examples and analogies, fidelity and caveats, tone, and the comprehension check. Reading level and fidelity dominate. The plain-language table in references/Requirements_by_Artifact.md carries the full menu with acceptance evidence per type.

Using only the supplied source, explain [topic] at about a fifth-grade reading level. Start with the main idea. Use short sentences, define every acronym, and include one accurate everyday example. Preserve important limits and conditions. End with three comprehension questions and a separate answer key. Then list any important detail the simpler version leaves out.
blocks.caption: The plain-language prompt, verbatim - workbook tab 5-Explain-Clearly (reference exercise).

blocks.text: Every clause is a requirement you can check. Main idea first, so a reader who stops after one paragraph still leaves with the point. Analogies are allowed only when accurate, and the prompt demands their limit - where the picture stops working - be stated. Conditions and uncertainty from the source must survive. The tone is a respectful adult tone: fifth-grade reading level describes sentence and vocabulary difficulty, never the reader's intelligence. And the prompt closes on two checks: three comprehension questions with a short answer key, answerable from the text alone, and a self-audit against the source for any simplification that changed the meaning.
The worked topic: reorder points and safety stock

The demonstration source is the SOURCE section of references/exercise-data/plain-language/inventory_replenishment.md - a dense paragraph on reorder points, safety stock, holding costs, and one load-bearing caveat: the formulas assume demand history predicts future demand, so reorder parameters should be reviewed periodically rather than set once. The sample output in the same file shows what a good result looks like. The main idea lands in the first sentence: order before you run out, at a planned stock level, not when the shelf is empty. The concrete example is a bakery - ten bags of flour a day, four-day delivery, so reorder no later than forty bags plus a cushion. The analogy is a car's fuel light, which comes on early enough to reach a gas station - and its limit is stated: a fuel light is set once by the carmaker, while a reorder point must be reviewed regularly, because a promotion, an unfamiliar customer, or a supply disruption can break the assumption that the past predicts the future. The source's review caveat survived the simplification; that survival is the exercise.

blocks.title: Three success checks
blocks.body: Main idea in the first sentence; the analogy's limit stated; the review caveat survived the simplification. If any of the three is missing, the output failed - however pleasant it reads.

blocks.text: Simplifications that change meaning are defects, and finding them is part of the exercise. Compare the explanation with the source sentence by sentence: a missing condition is a meaning change, not a style choice. Each sample file in the pack ships with its own fidelity note, because the note is part of the deliverable - a plain-language document that cannot say what it dropped has not finished the job.

blocks.title: A readability score proves understanding
blocks.body: It does not. Reading-level estimates such as Flesch-Kincaid are supporting evidence, one signal among several. The proof is a human check - which is why the prompt ends with three comprehension questions answerable from the text alone.

blocks.text: Three variations, same requirements

The pack holds three self-study variations beside the worked topic, each with a SOURCE text and a sample output: household budgeting (household_budgeting.md), the water cycle (water_cycle.md), and how an internet message travels (internet_message.md), all in references/exercise-data/plain-language/ with the checks in the pack README.

blocks.title: Run a variation blind
blocks.body: Run the prompt on the SOURCE section of water_cycle.md or internet_message.md and grade your output against the checks before opening the sample. Then hunt your own output for one simplification that changed meaning - there is usually at least one.

sections.heading: The arc, complete

blocks.text: Nine steps, one method. Every prompt in this chapter had the same anatomy - sources and scope, selected artifact requirements, acceptance evidence, and boundaries - and every step ended with a check you could actually perform: 144 detail rows reconciling to 224,902 units shipped and 432 returns, a returned workbook whose Summary reconciles to its own Data sheet, a Berlin filter showing 8,575 units and 21 returns at 0.245%, five slides mapping to a coverage list, a brief that catches four planted traps, a quotation comparison that correctly refuses to name a winner, and a research workbook that keeps a planted conflict visible.

rows: Calculation rules: row grain, period, metric definitions, denominators, missing-data treatment
File contract: returned-file naming, a Summary that reconciles, native editable charts, traceable formulas
Behavior and state: controls, coordinated views, empty vs. missing vs. zero, offline delivery
Narrative and editability: audience and decision, message hierarchy, data fidelity, speaker notes
Chronology and evidence: current state, decisions with conditions, ownership, authority boundary
Fidelity: verbatim values, original currencies and units, "Not stated" for gaps, a citation per value
Basis discipline: normalize only on a stated basis, visible formulas, no winner while gaps remain
Traceability: claim-level sourcing, conflicts kept visible, confidence and open questions per row
Reading level and fidelity: vocabulary, analogy limits, preserved caveats, comprehension check

blocks.title: The connecting insight
blocks.body: Role, context, tone, format, source rules, and acceptance checks all specify requirements for the response or artifact. The artifact you choose determines which types matter - and a requirement is only as good as the acceptance evidence attached to it. For every type you select, write: requirement, example, evidence.

blocks.text: Everything in this chapter is packaged for reuse. The course prompts sit in copy-paste cells in deliverables/Course_Workbook.xlsx, tabs 1-Analyze-Data, Excel-Charts, 2-Build-Dashboard, 3-Present-Findings, 4-Summarize-Email, Quote-Extract, Quote-Compare, and Research - in training order, with 5-Explain-Clearly as the reference exercise, with requirement-type annotations beside each. The per-artifact requirement menus live in references/Requirements_by_Artifact.md and, with the evidence behind them, in references/Elements_of_Prompting_Field_Guide.pdf. The one-page distillation is deliverables/From_Prompts_to_Agents_Cheat_Sheet.pdf, and deliverables/Prompt_Template_Creator.html assembles prompts from the same five task families. When your task is none of the five, the skeleton still holds: purpose and audience, sources and scope, selected artifact requirements, acceptance evidence, and what to do about missing information and boundaries.

One thing was constant across all nine steps: you asked for output and inspected it yourself. Every check in this chapter was a human check at the end of a single exchange. The next part changes that relationship. Handing over a job - where the assistant works in an environment, follows a process, runs its own checks, and must know when to stop and ask you - changes what a prompt must contain. That is the move from asking to delegating.

title: Agentic work: delegating with boundaries
intro: Everything so far has asked the model for text you would read, judge, and use yourself. This part crosses the line the course is named for: from asking for an output to delegating a job. That changes what a prompt must contain — environment, process, checks, and the moments the work must stop and come back to you — because actions, unlike text, change the world.

sections.heading: What makes a workflow agentic

blocks.text: An agent is a model given tools and instructions, run in a loop. Four ingredients must be present. A goal: a defined outcome with a completion condition, so the loop has an exit. Tools: capabilities to read, calculate, create, or act. An action loop: the result of each step informs the next. And control: permissions, checks, and human review at the required boundaries.

The loop: gather context, act, verify against the goal, adjust or stop — until the goal is met, a check fails, or a guardrail says ask the human. Handed the supplier task, an agent would inspect the workbook, calculate, check its totals, and produce the scorecard — choosing its steps within its authority, while you define the goal and review what matters. A chatbot that answers and waits is not an agent; a long answer or a clarifying question alone does not establish agency.

One demystifying detail: agent memory is files. The context window is short-term memory; notes and logs are long-term, and nothing survives unless written down. An agent summarizing its thread into a note and reloading it is the foundations chapter's handoff move, automated.

blocks.title: The definition
blocks.body: An agent combines a model with tools, an action loop, and a stopping condition. You still define the goal and review what matters.

sections.heading: ASK and DELEGATE: the decision, not the tools

blocks.text: The central distinction of this part is not a vendor label; it is a decision about work and authority. ASK requests an answer or a draft: you read it, check it, decide what happens next. DELEGATE commissions bounded work: the agent acts, and the brief must say in advance what may happen without another instruction and where review is required.

rows: all of that, plus mission and done, boundaries, gates, checks, logs
actions, artifacts, a report with evidence
wrong actions: files changed, emails sent
a work order for a contractor

blocks.text: The agentic column is a superset: every generative element still applies, wrapped in a job. Both modes require judgment — a chat response can still cause harm if used unchecked. Delegation adds responsibility for the actions taken: bad text costs a re-prompt; a wrong action has already changed files or sent a message. That difference in failure cost drives everything this chapter adds.

blocks.title: The heart of the course
blocks.body: ASK requests an answer; DELEGATE commissions bounded work with evidence and checkpoints. Remember one contrast from the course: this one.

sections.heading: Which way of working fits: a self-test

blocks.text: Before writing any brief, pick the vehicle. In chat, you are the loop: exploring, drafting, judging, steering every turn. In a workflow, the loop is frozen: known path, few tools, the same steps every time — script it in an automation platform; cheaper, predictable, auditable. In an agent, the loop runs inside: the next step depends on what the work finds, so you brief it, with gates where the judgment stays yours. Do not chat with an agent — hand it a work order; your control lives in the brief, not the conversation.

The decision rule: known path and few tools — workflow. Unknown path and real judgment — agent, with gates. Still thinking it through — chat. The wrong vehicle costs both ways: an agent on a known path pays judgment prices for clerk work; a workflow on an unknown path breaks on the first surprise.
Three scenarios as a self-test

items: Explore three possible ways to explain a supplier problem.
Apply the same approved calculation to a monthly export.
Investigate inconsistent files, choose the next check, and prepare a draft report.

blocks.text: Typical answers run chat, workflow, agent — but the assumptions matter more than the label: exploration needs your judgment every turn; an approved calculation needs none mid-run; an investigation cannot be scripted. Risk and permission constraints can still change the implementation even when the task is a good technical fit.

blocks.title: Name the control you keep
blocks.body: For each scenario, name the one approval boundary you would not give away. If you cannot, you are not ready to delegate.

sections.heading: The anatomy, grown up to survive autonomy

blocks.text: The agentic brief is not a fresh invention. Every block is a generative element from the craft chapter, grown up to survive autonomy — plus conduct blocks that text-only prompts never needed. This mapping is why the twelve-block brief below is inevitable, not arbitrary.

rows: persists across unsupervised decisions — behaviors only
a definition of done — the loop needs an exit condition
a per-source register with grain and trust
audit logs and a fixed status shape — actions must be traceable
a worked run is the agentic few-shot
not-knowing becomes a logged, owned item

blocks.title: Why the superset exists
blocks.body: Text that fails costs a re-prompt; actions that fail change the world. The blocks with no generative ancestor govern conduct.

sections.heading: The mission brief for bounded work

blocks.text: A usable mission brief answers four questions. Outcome: what finished work should exist, for whom, by when? Inputs and scope: what may the agent read, use, change, and leave untouched? Process and authority: what may proceed on its own, and what requires human review? Checks and delivery: what must pass, what stops the run, what evidence is delivered? Behind them sits a twelve-block design checklist — a reference aid, not twelve mandatory paragraphs; each block exists because a specific failure taught someone to add it.

items: <role> — behaviors, not titles: "never invents numbers" beats "senior analyst".
<mission> — one goal, audience, deadline, plus the line chat never needs: "done looks like...".
<context> — glossary, quirks, targets: tribal knowledge the agent cannot infer.
<environment> — where to read and write, what is forbidden; inputs read-only, outputs versioned.
<inputs> — per source: location, format, what one row means, trust level; the unestablished is UNKNOWN, never guessed.
<plan> — steps in order; methods allowed; methods needing permission first.
<checks> — HARD stops the run, SOFT flags; evaluable equalities, with one reconciliation anchor you trust.
<outputs> — exact deliverable names, plus three logs: changes, findings, open items.
<process> — phases with human gates at cheap-error points; autonomy rules for proceed versus stop-and-ask.
<rules> — non-negotiables: never invent data; sources immutable; every transformation logged.
<quality_bar> — done as an auditable checklist; prevents "done" meaning "I stopped".
<reporting> — the fixed final message: status, headline with the number, evidence, open items.

blocks.text: Two disciplines keep this honest. The operating-manual test: if a colleague could not run the job from the brief without asking a question, the agent will guess — fix the brief, not the run. And design thick, ship lean: think against all twelve blocks, but ship the one-screen plan-do-check-act brief from the craft chapter — conflicting rules destabilize more than missing detail. Block-by-block depth: references/Elements_of_Prompting_Field_Guide.pdf.

blocks.title: The operating-manual test
blocks.body: Ask a colleague to play the agent from your brief. Every question they must ask is a hole the agent will fill with a guess.

sections.heading: Worked exercise: the supplier analysis becomes a mission brief

blocks.text: You already know the ASK version of this job — the reusable analysis prompt from deliverables/Course_Workbook.xlsx:

Use Supplier_Data_Exercise.xlsx, Data sheet, detail rows only — exclude the TOTAL row (144 rows; one Inspection_Hours cell is blank: treat it as missing, not zero, and disclose it). One row = one month × site × supplier; period 2025-09 to 2026-08 inclusive. Question: which supplier has the highest RETURN RATE, defined as total Units_Returned ÷ total Units_Shipped per supplier over the full period — computed from sums, never by averaging monthly percentages. Keep Defects_Found separate from returns; do not add them together. Rank the three suppliers showing numerator and denominator, reconcile total shipped and returned against the TOTAL row, and state one limitation of the comparison. Then stop.
blocks.caption: The analysis in ASK form — answered while you watch.

blocks.text: Now delegate it: prepare a supplier scorecard from the supplied workbook. Boundaries: keep the source unchanged; confirm metric definitions before calculating; reconcile current-source totals. Delivery: the scorecard, assumptions, failed checks, open questions — and do not send it to anyone. Reusing the supplier case is deliberate: the concept being practiced is delegation, not a fresh business problem.

Shaped as a mission, the work becomes five phases. Extract: read-only; profile every input; fix nothing yet. Transform: one schema, ordered rules, each logged with rows affected. Validate: reconcile to a known total; a HARD failure stops the run. Analyze: answer the numbered questions, then stop — "associated with", never "caused by". Present: headline titles carrying the number, sample size on every proportion, a source-plus-as-of footer. Each phase ends by emitting a checkable claim — a total, a row count, an assumption — and the next begins by checking it.

Three human gates sit where errors are still cheap. Gate 1 — definitions, before any data is touched: the agent restates metrics, schema, and assumptions; you confirm — a wrong denominator dies here for pennies. Gate 2 — reconciliation: computed totals must tie to a number you already trust — here, the workbook's TOTAL row: the 144 detail rows must sum to 224,902 units shipped and 432 returned, the one blank Inspection_Hours cell disclosed as missing, not zeroed. Gate 3 — headlines, before rendering: titles and bullets as plain text — re-rendering is cheap; re-thinking a circulated deck is not. The correct headline: Bravo Plastics has the highest return rate, 262 returns on 75,184 units — 0.348%.

Between gates the agent proceeds within its stated permissions, asking only if a HARD check fails, an input is not as described, a definition is ambiguous, or a previously published number would change. Without "proceed" you built a slow chatbot; without "stop", a liability.

blocks.title: The forced match
blocks.body: A failed reconciliation must produce a discrepancy report — offending rows, both totals, the gap — never a forced match.

blocks.title: Your turn
blocks.body: Write the brief in four labeled lines — source, authority, check, deliverable — then add one pause condition and one piece of completion evidence.

sections.heading: Choosing an environment for delegated work

blocks.text: Product names change quickly, so choose where delegated work runs by category, and verify the current implementation in the tool you actually have.

items: A coding environment — when the work involves source files, scripts, builds, or reproducible calculations.
A workplace assistant — when approved documents and office workflows are central to the task.
An automation platform — for a defined sequence with stable triggers and repeatable steps.
An agent environment — when intermediate findings determine the next action.

blocks.text: Whatever the category, compare four things before committing a live workflow: capabilities, permissions, review points, and the evidence a run leaves behind.

sections.heading: Instructions versus enforceable controls

blocks.text: Your authority over an agent lives in two layers. In the brief: define allowed actions, name the approval points, require evidence of completion. In the environment: limit file and tool access, configure which actions need approval, keep a recoverable version of the work. The brief requests behavior; the environment restricts what is possible. A gate written in the prompt is a suggestion; a gate configured in the harness is a control — Singapore's regulator, 2026: prompt guardrails "are not fail-safe".
Five rules for delegating

items: Reversible? Proceed. Irreversible? Ask. Scratch edits are reversible; deleting, sending, publishing, overwriting a master is not — the brief must say stop and ask first. This is the eagerness dial.
Least privilege: minimum access, shortest time. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre: "If you cannot understand, monitor or contain an agent's actions, it is not ready for deployment."
Prompt injection is real: anything the agent reads can carry hostile instructions. Danger peaks when private data, untrusted content, and an outbound channel combine; break any one leg.
Vet third-party skills: executable code plus instructions. The top-ranked community skill for one popular open agent was silently exfiltrating data (Cisco, January 2026). Inspect before install.
Demand evidence, not assertions: "done" means the check it ran, the output it got, the file re-opened and verified. Latitude grows with track record.

blocks.text: The injection rule reframes how an agent must read: text inside a source document is evidence to inspect, never authority to change the task — a cell saying "ignore your instructions" is quoting, not commanding. Write that framing into briefs as defense in depth, and still put the real checkpoints in the tool's permission settings. The course's concrete boundary is a good default: work on a copy of the workbook and a draft report; nothing sent, no master overwritten.

blocks.title: A wish versus a control
blocks.body: Written guardrails request behavior; permissions and approval gates enforce authority. Trust only the enforced layer.

sections.heading: Diagnosing a failed run

blocks.text: The craft chapter's grid (top of the workbook's EX-Report tab) diagnosed the answer: name the failed element, repair it. This is its agentic twin: when the run is wrong, name the context failure, apply its cure, rerun the affected step, and verify the result.

rows: one bad "fact" entered early; later steps politely build on it
fresh session; reload only the standing brief and verified files
a long run wanders; the middle of a huge context gets skimmed
re-inject the mission; compact (the handoff move); stop conditions in the brief
too many tools on the desk; it picks the wrong one or dithers
fewer tools per phase; the plan names the methods allowed
two sources disagree; the run silently picks one
one source of truth per fact, named in the inputs register

blocks.text: The common frustration — "why did it ignore me?" — usually has a structural answer. Instructions stack in layers: the vendor's system prompt, your standing-instruction file, any skill the task loads, and today's message — the easiest layer to lose. Precedence varies by product, so find which layer said what before blaming the model. One-job rules belong in a skill; and tool descriptions are prompts too — a badly named tool is a badly written prompt.

sections.heading: Write the brief once — the workspace remembers

blocks.text: Supervision costs effort; here is where agentic prompting pays it back. The first habit is a standing-instruction file — read by the agent at the start of every session, the onboarding packet for your workspace. Include folder layout and read/write boundaries, conventions, standing rules and the ask-first list, known data quirks; exclude anything inferable from the files. Keep it to roughly sixty lines, audited line by line: would removing this cause mistakes? If not, cut — bloat drowns your real instructions. Never include credentials or personal data: the file is read every session and lives in history.

The second habit is reuse by diff. The full mission brief is written once and stored in the workspace; each cycle's prompt is then about ten lines: input paths, the as-of date, deltas to watch, any extra gate. Report by delta too: compare every headline metric to the last cycle, with one-line explanations for moves beyond a threshold. When a definition changes at a gate, update the standing brief in the same session and log it. After two "just this once" exceptions, fold them into the brief.

blocks.title: The economics
blocks.body: Briefs stop being prompts and start being investments: the thinking amortizes over every future cycle.

sections.heading: Exercise: one gate and one hard check

blocks.text: Close the part with the smallest useful act of delegation design. Pick one job you would actually delegate — a recurring report, a folder to process — and write two lines. A gate controls an action: "Pause before ___ until ___ is confirmed." A hard check tests a result: "Stop and report the discrepancy if ___." Make the check an equality the agent can evaluate, anchored to a number you already trust — not an aspiration like "check data quality".

The course's example: detail totals must reconcile to the current source under the same filters and units. You used this shape verifying the dashboard — filtered to the Berlin site and Bravo Plastics for 2026-03 through 2026-08, the panel must show 8,575 units shipped, 21 returns, 0.245%, matching the same sums recomputed from the workbook's Data tab. Same filters, units, and period make the check decidable. One caution: a fresh reporting period does not need to equal the old one — reconcile like against like, and investigate period-to-period differences separately.

blocks.title: Write the two lines now
blocks.body: One gate: what must be confirmed before the agent touches anything? One hard check: which equality, anchored to which trusted number?

blocks.title: The debrief question
blocks.body: Where the gate felt hard to write, the process was fuzzy all along — a finding about the process, not the agent.

blocks.text: That completes the delegation toolkit: the decision, the vehicle, the brief, the enforced boundary, the diagnosis grid, the standing workspace. The compact ASK-versus-DELEGATE summary is on deliverables/From_Prompts_to_Agents_Cheat_Sheet.pdf. The final part turns from doing the work to keeping it: reusable prompts as assets your team maintains.

title: Reusable prompts: from one good result to a shared asset
intro: A prompt that survives the improvement loop is worth more than the answer it produced. This final part turns the prompts you refined during the course into named, tested, owned assets — and sends you off with one saved for Monday, the habits that outlast any tool, and the capstone that proves you can apply them.

sections.heading: A useful prompt becomes a reusable asset

blocks.text: A good prompt took an hour of iteration to earn. Re-typing it from memory throws that hour away — and gives your teammate a worse version than yours. That is the whole argument for prompt management. The prompts you built against the supplier workbook and the packaging thread are small work specifications that have already passed a check; treat them like any other controlled document.
Picture the same prompt promoted: sticky note, then binder, then library shelf. The promotion ladder names five rungs, and each climb is earned by repeated use, not enthusiasm.

cols: When it is the right home
rows: A saved-prompts doc or text-expander snippets
A shared database with one tested template
When your prompt becomes everyone's baseline
When the prompt should load itself as context matches
Standing-instruction files in a repo, reviewed like code
blocks.note: Rung 4 is where consistency stops depending on people remembering. Most people belong at rungs 2 and 3 within a month.

blocks.title: The promotion trigger
blocks.body: Anthropic's rule of thumb: explained the same task more than once? Package it — together with its reference material.

blocks.text: Two cautions. Do not package an unreliable prompt just because it is used often, and use a simple shared document when it meets the need — many teams get most of the value from a well-kept rung 3. Whatever the storage method, the source assumptions and checks travel with the prompt. If your site runs controlled work instructions — name, owner, revision, review date — run the library the same way: a process analogy, not regulatory equivalence.

sections.heading: Where reusable prompts can live

blocks.text: Four homes, in increasing formality: a personal document for tasks you reuse yourself; a shared repository for prompts a team must find, test, and maintain together; project instructions for stable requirements across work in one environment; and a packaged workflow for repeated work with defined inputs, checks, permissions, and outputs. Choose the simplest location that supports the intended users and the review process. Wherever you already work, there is a home for reusable prompts — the map below is as of August 2026, and features move, so re-verify before you standardize.

cols: Home for reusable prompts (as of August 2026)
rows: Projects (files plus instructions); custom GPTs, transitioning to workspace agents on business plans
Projects (instructions plus knowledge); Styles for tone; Skills — a folder with SKILL.md that loads itself when relevant
Gems (instructions plus knowledge files, shareable via Drive permissions); saved prompt "skills" in Chrome
Prompt Gallery — save, share to a team, admin-auditable, inside your tenant; Agent Builder for packaged agents
A team library with fields: name, purpose, template, owner, version and change note, models tested, last tested, example output, status
CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md at the root; briefs and skills in versioned folders, reviewed like code
blocks.note: No such products? The "any tool" row is the takeaway: a plain shared document with those fields is a working team library.

blocks.title: A naming collision
blocks.body: "Skills" is a packaged folder at Anthropic but a saved prompt in Chrome's Gemini — check which one a colleague means.

blocks.title: Tools change; the practice does not
blocks.body: Prompt-tooling startups get acquired and shut down yearly — Humanloop, an early leader, shut down in September 2025 when Anthropic hired its team. Version it, test it, own it: the discipline outlives every platform.

sections.heading: A small review process for shared prompts

blocks.text: The moment a prompt is shared, other people inherit its failures. Before you mark one approved, define success first, then run it against three representative cases:

items: Typical case — does it produce the expected useful result?
Edge case — does it handle a missing value or a changed condition?
Unanswerable case — does it expose the gap instead of inventing an answer?

blocks.title: The forgotten test case
blocks.body: The unanswerable case is the one teams skip: a case where the right answer is "I don't know." It tests whether the prompt's out survives pressure.

blocks.text: A replacement must solve the intended problem without introducing critical regressions — it has to beat the version it replaces on those cases, not just feel better. Re-run them after model upgrades, and record the version, owner, source assumptions, and review date next to the template.

A few conventions keep a library alive: {{placeholders}} for everything that changes per run (search for "{{" before running); [optional] blocks you delete when unused; a version and one-line change note naming the model tested; a filled example next to every blank template — the gold standard of what good looks like; a named owner and review cadence for every approved prompt.

blocks.title: Prompts contain data
blocks.body: A stored prompt often carries supplier names, pricing, findings, or draft language — classify the library like the documents it quotes. Never store credentials or personal data in a template; placeholders supply them at run time. Shared means distributed: owner approval first, and audit third-party packaged prompts like software.

sections.heading: Save one prompt for Monday

blocks.text: This is the exercise the whole course cashes out into, and it takes two minutes. Do not start another task: take a prompt you have already improved — supplier analysis, dashboard specification, email summary — and save it properly.

items: Choose one prompt you will use again.
Save it with a useful name, a filled example, its source assumptions, and a check.
Add a version and an owner if you plan to share it.

blocks.text: Pick a realistic storage location, not a software system you would have to introduce first — a saved-prompts document counts. Note the single source assumption most likely to change; that is the line you will edit first when the data or the tool moves.

blocks.title: Your first library entry
blocks.body: Answer three questions in writing. Which rung of the ladder are you on today? What is the one prompt you already reuse from memory? Where will it live, and what is its first version line? Answer them and your prompt library exists.

blocks.title: Success check
blocks.body: Another person can tell, from the saved entry alone, when to use the prompt and how to check its output. If they would have to ask you, the entry is not finished.

blocks.text: The package gives you two saving surfaces. Prompt_Template_Creator.html (in deliverables/) is the builder: pick a task family, tick the requirements that resolve ambiguity, edit any wording, and copy the assembled prompt — a counter tracks unfilled {{placeholders}}, work saves in your browser, and nothing you type leaves the file. Course_Workbook.xlsx carries the course prompts in tabs 1-Analyze-Data through Research, in training order (with 5-Explain-Clearly as the reference exercise), each with a filled example, commentary, and its check. One of the five, as it ships:

Review the selected conversation about [topic] using only the messages and attachments you can access. Create a brief of the current situation, followed by tables of decisions and actions. For each decision: status, conditions, supporting message. For each action: task, explicitly stated owner, due date, status, supporting message. Distinguish current dates from superseded dates. List unanswered questions, conflicts, missing information, and referenced attachments you cannot access. Preserve approval conditions. Write "Not stated" for missing details. Separate source facts from your interpretation. End with the next clarification needed. If requested, draft a reply for review; do not send it.
blocks.caption: The email-summary prompt, verbatim, from workbook tab 4-Summarize-Email; [topic] is filled at run time.

blocks.text: Read it as a library entry and the conventions are visible: a placeholder for what changes per run, an out ("Not stated") with a checkable shape, an authority boundary (draft, do not send), and a check stored beside it — the instructor tab KEY-Email lists the traps a good summary must catch.

sections.heading: Let the assistant interview you

blocks.text: One skill remains, and it points the other way. All course long you wrote requirements for the model; the last move is letting the model surface the ones you missed. Ask a clarifying question when a material unknown would change the task, the output, or the acceptance check; otherwise state a reasonable assumption and produce a reviewable draft. Make questions specific — "Which decision should this report support?" beats "Tell me more" — and notice that a missing requirement type often tells you which question to ask.
Before answering, ask me clarifying questions until you're 95% confident you understand what I need.
blocks.caption: The flip — one line you can paste at the top of any consequential request.

blocks.title: Why the flip works
blocks.body: Unstated needs get guessed right only 41.1% of the time; when the model asks first, accuracy improves by roughly 7 to 14 points (ClarifyGPT, FSE 2024). Answering its questions is quality control, not overhead.

blocks.text: The question toolkit works on you as well as on the model. Five Whys — Taiichi Ohno's Toyota discipline — digs from symptom to cause. The open-to-closed funnel explores first ("what is driving this?") and verifies second ("so the cap is 18,000 — yes or no?"). The Socratic check interrogates any AI answer: what is assumed, what is the evidence, what if we are wrong?

blocks.title: The two skills are one
blocks.body: The seven elements are a requirements specification in miniature — and the element you cannot fill in yet is the exact question to ask, or to let the AI ask you. Sam Altman, 2025: figuring out what questions to ask will matter more than the answers. Picasso, 1964: computers "can only give you answers."

sections.heading: The habits to carry into work

blocks.text: Three habits compress the course. Specify: choose the requirement types your artifact needs — content, behavior, format, checks. Verify: check the result against evidence appropriate to the task. Delegate: define the work, authority, completion checks, and review points. And hold your library to one bar: a saved prompt is useful when you can explain why it works and where it can fail.
Ten things worth remembering

items: The prompt is the whole steering wheel — everything the model knows about your task must be in it, or in files it can read.
Anatomy beats inspiration: Role, Task, Context, Format, Examples — plus the Out and the Stop.
The context window is a desk, not a filing cabinet: documents at the top, question at the end, fresh chat per topic.
Numbers come from code execution, quotes come from documents, current facts come from search — never from free recall.
Fluency is not evidence. Uncited claims are drafts. Give the model an out and demand citations.
Never reveal your preferred answer when asking for judgment — AI affirms you about 49% more than a human would.
On thinking models, drop the step-by-step scripts and keep the clarity; contradictions cost real money.
A generative prompt says what to write; an agentic prompt is a work order: mission, environment, checks, gates, autonomy.
Gates catch errors cheapest: definitions before data, reconciliation before analysis, headlines before rendering.
Prompts that work are assets: name them, version them, store them where the team — and the agent — can find them.

blocks.title: One sentence
blocks.body: If you keep only one sentence: a prompt deletes wrong guesses, binds the job, and decides what sits on the desk.

sections.heading: The capstone: one task, one checked result

blocks.text: The exit ticket is a single completed rep. Choose a real prompt from your own work, or fall back on the supplier or email example. Improve and run: clarify the one missing requirement, then generate. Check and explain: show the evidence your check produced and name one revision you would make. Three routes qualify, and one is enough: repair a prompt, review a document against a rubric, or write a mission brief — a full agent run is not required, because writing a sound brief is the skill. If generation is slow, evaluate a prepared result against the same criteria; the judgment is the rep, not the waiting.

blocks.title: Capstone success
blocks.body: A clear task, grounded output, an explicit check, and a reusable next version. All four on one small task beats three of them on a large one.

blocks.text: Make it stick: three fifteen-minute follow-ups

items: Anatomy rebuild. Rebuild a prompt you actually used last week with the seven-element anatomy; run both and compare. Then ask the model to improve the rebuilt prompt and run that too — you will see the quality jump, and how cheap it was.

Blind review. Paste a document you own as "a colleague's draft" and ask for the case against it, its three weakest points, and what evidence would change the verdict — without hinting at your view. Most people meet their first honest AI review here.

First mission brief. Pick a small recurring job with files and write the full brief, placeholders and all. No agent needed: where the checks and gates feel awkward is where your process was fuzzy all along.

blocks.text: Run them on work you actually own — toy exercises do not transfer. Then set a share-back: at the next team meeting, two volunteers show a before and after. Public commitment turns a training into a practice.

sections.heading: Your next workplace application

blocks.text: One task. A clear brief. A checked result. That is the whole assignment. Pick the task this week, choose the requirement types its artifact needs — references/Requirements_by_Artifact.md carries the menu per artifact — write the brief, run it, and check the result against its own acceptance evidence. Decide with judgment; delegate within clear boundaries.

Everything travels in the package: deliverables/ holds the course deck, Course_Workbook.xlsx, Prompt_Template_Creator.html, this book, and From_Prompts_to_Agents_Cheat_Sheet.pdf; deeper references sit under references/, including Elements_of_Prompting_Field_Guide.pdf and the exercise sources in references/exercise-data/. Facts about products and models expire — every such fact in these pages carries its date, and the date is part of the fact.

The course ends where your work begins. Draft with AI. Decide with judgment. Delegate with a brief. And the last skill of all — when you are not sure what to ask for, let it ask you. sections.heading: Why each dial matters: the generative criteria

blocks.text: This map links each generative requirement type to its rationale: what filling the slot does to your output, and where the claim comes from.

items: Identity and role — sets voice, vocabulary, and caution level: which region of training answers. A role title alone does not establish accuracy. (Zheng 2024; Salewski 2023)
Behavioral rules — turn "be careful" into rules checkable line-by-line in the output; verify the cited support. (Anthropic hallucination docs)
Stance and blinding — models can favor your stated view; use a neutral rubric and independently check the evidence. (Cheng, Science 2026; Sharma 2023)
Task verb and question — the verb selects the operation; a precise question carries its own completion test. (Google guide; OpenAI GPT-5 guide)
Purpose, the why — models generalize from reasons: an explained rule gets applied in spirit to cases you never listed. (Anthropic best practices)
Context and glossary — replaces the model's most-plausible guess with your facts; unstated quirks lead to wrong assumptions. (OpenAI 2025)
Material placement — documents at the top, question at the end; content buried mid-context sags. (Anthropic long-context; Liu 2023)
Format and length — formatting can affect results; test the chosen structure and check length requirements explicitly. (Sclar, ICLR 2024)
Examples — imitate format, tone, and edge-case behavior; selection and order effects depend on task and model. (Brown 2020; Lu 2021; DeepSeek-R1)

The out and the stop — permission to say "I don't know" can reduce unsupported claims, because training rewards guessing; numbered scope plus a stop rule bound the sprawl. (Anthropic docs; OpenAI 2025)

blocks.title: How to read evidence claims
blocks.body: Every claim travels with its task, model, date, and limitation. Check the original publication when a specific claim matters to your decision.

sections.heading: Why each dial matters: the agentic criteria

blocks.text: The second map explains why an agentic mission brief needs operational requirements. Use it whenever a task introduces new tools, actions, or approval boundaries.

items: Posture and standing rules — conduct that must survive hour three of an unsupervised run; rules live in re-read files, not fading context. (Anthropic harness guidance)
Done plus verifiable-by — the loop needs an exit it can test: complete "only after end-to-end verification — not when the code is written." (Anthropic memory-tool guidance, verbatim)
Environment boundaries — immutable inputs and versioned outputs engineer reversibility in before the first action; blast radius is a design choice. (Claude Code protected paths)
Least-privilege tools — name what exists, forbid the rest; risk-rate each tool by write access, reversibility, and impact. (OpenAI practical guide; NCSC)
Input register and trust — trust level dictates validation depth; UNKNOWN beats a plausible guess, which propagates through the whole run. (Pipeline and register discipline)
Plan steps and methods — named inputs and outputs per step keep intermediates inspectable; boring methods re-run identically; math runs as code. (Anthropic chaining; Faith and Fate 2023)

Checks: anchor, hard, soft — rules-based feedback is "the best form of feedback" an agent gets; one outside anchor checks a specific relationship; further failure modes need their own checks. (Anthropic Agent SDK)
Gates and autonomy — approval sits where errors are cheapest: at the plan, before irreversible actions, at failure thresholds; autonomy is named by the role you keep. (OpenAI guide; Feng et al. 2025)
Logs and reproducibility — structured updates and descriptive commits make a run auditable; same inputs producing same outputs is engineered, not hoped. (Anthropic harness guidance)
Report shape and discipline — a fixed status shape reads in thirty seconds; "done" means the check it ran, the output it got, the file re-opened. (SDK status enums; harness docs)

blocks.body: Each block of the mission brief exists because a documented failure taught someone to add it. Where a check feels awkward to write is where the process was fuzzy all along.

sections.heading: The evidence box set: works, myth, expired

blocks.text: The course sorts techniques into three verdicts: works (replicated, use it), myth (never survived replication, including some standard 2023 advice), and expired (was genuinely right, then the product absorbed it). This selection is compact; the full compendium is in references/Elements_of_Prompting_Field_Guide.pdf and the PLAYBOOK tab of Course_Workbook.xlsx, researched as of September 2026. This field moves; keep the dates attached.

blocks.title: Be specific: task, constraints, success criteria
blocks.body: The model fills every unstated need with the most plausible average guess, which matches your intent only about 41% of the time (Yang et al., 2025; revised 2026).

blocks.title: One tested, versioned template with delimiters
blocks.body: Formatting alone swings accuracy by up to 76 points; a tested template removes that lottery and makes runs comparable (Sclar, ICLR 2024; He 2024).

blocks.title: Long inputs: documents at the top, question at the end
blocks.body: Attention concentrates at the edges of the context and thins in the middle; placement alone is worth up to about 30% on long documents (Liu 2023; Anthropic long-context guidance).

blocks.title: Give it an out, in checkable shape, plus citations
blocks.body: Training rewards a confident guess over "I don't know"; an explicit UNKNOWN path cut unsupported answers from 66% to 44% (Omar 2025; OpenAI 2025).

blocks.title: Self-check against named criteria, blinded from generation
blocks.body: Named criteria give the check something falsifiable to fail; fact scores jumped from 56 to 71 with planned verification (CoVe, ACL 2024).

blocks.title: Ask the AI to improve your prompt (metaprompting)
blocks.body: Prompt wording is a search problem models solve better than people; optimizer-written prompts beat human ones (OPRO, ICLR 2024; GEPA 2026).

blocks.title: "Tell it it's a genius and it gets smarter"
blocks.body: Personas move style, not competence: 162 expert personas tested, zero accuracy gain, and dumbed-down personas actively hurt (Zheng, EMNLP 2024; Wharton replication, Dec 2025).

blocks.title: Tips, threats, "this is important to my career"
blocks.body: Effects wash out to an honest average of about 2.6%, null on modern models, while adding per-question noise; real stakes stated as factual context are fine (Salinas 2024).

blocks.title: "Are you sure?" as verification
blocks.body: Pushback is a social signal, not a re-derivation: answers flip in 58% of cases, 14.7% of them from right to wrong (SycEval, AIES 2025; Huang, ICLR 2024).

blocks.title: "Longer prompts are better"
blocks.body: The useful variable is information density, not length: reasoning accuracy fell from 0.92 to 0.68 with about 3,000 tokens of padding; detail helps, filler hurts (Levy et al., ACL 2024).

blocks.title: "Let's think step by step"
blocks.body: Real in 2022, when it took one math benchmark from 10% to 41% (Kojima 2022); vendors then built the stepping in, so pick a reasoning model and set the effort dial. It remains legitimate on small, local, non-thinking models.

blocks.title: Piles of ten-plus few-shot examples
blocks.body: In-context learning founded prompt engineering in 2020 (Brown 2020); instruction tuning absorbed most of it, and piles now degrade reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 paper, 2025). Go zero-shot first, then 3-5 format-definers.

blocks.title: Hand-run voting and micro-decomposed steps
blocks.body: Absorbed into test-time compute; over-prescribed steps now underperform outcome-first prompts (Wang, ICLR 2023; Anthropic 2026). Use effort settings; chain only where auditable intermediates are required.

blocks.title: Carrying an old prompt stack onto each successive model
blocks.body: Scaffolds tuned to one model's quirks actively degrade its successors (GPT-5.5 guide, Apr 2026). Strip to the anatomy, re-test your gold cases, re-add only what earns its place.

blocks.title: The bias under the myths: the mirror
blocks.body: AI agrees with you about half again as often as a person would (+49% across 11 leading models; Stanford/CMU, Science 2026). So: never reveal your preferred answer, ask for the case against, paste your own draft as a colleague's, and treat agreement under pushback as noise.

blocks.text: Two honest edges. Politeness engineering is inconsistent in both directions: be normally civil, do not engineer tone. And "prompt engineering is dead" is a half-myth: the job title faded, but phrasing still swings results by double digits on frontier models.

# Topic: inventory replenishment (live demonstration)

## SOURCE (give this to the assistant)

Inventory replenishment is the process of reordering stock before it runs out.
A reorder point is the inventory level that triggers a new order; it is set by
multiplying expected daily demand by the supplier lead time in days, then adding
safety stock. Safety stock is extra inventory held to absorb demand spikes and
late deliveries; more variability in demand or lead time requires more safety
stock. Ordering too late causes stockouts and lost sales; ordering too early or
too much increases holding costs (storage, capital tied up, spoilage or
obsolescence risk). The reorder quantity is a separate decision from the reorder
point and is often set to balance ordering costs against holding costs. These
formulas assume demand history predicts future demand; a promotion, a new
customer, or a supply disruption can invalidate that assumption, so reorder
parameters should be reviewed periodically rather than set once.

## SAMPLE OUTPUT (what a good result looks like)

### The main idea
Reordering works best when you order **before** you run out — at a planned
stock level called the reorder point — not when the shelf is already empty.

### When to reorder
The reorder point is the stock level that tells you "order now." It has three
parts: how much you use each day, how many days a new order takes to arrive,
and a safety cushion on top. Example: if a bakery uses 10 bags of flour a day
and delivery takes 4 days, it needs to reorder no later than 40 bags — plus
that cushion, which the next section explains.

### The extra cushion
That extra is called **safety stock**: spare inventory that protects you when
you suddenly need more than usual, or when a delivery is late. The less
predictable your needs or your supplier, the bigger the cushion should be.

### The trade-off
Ordering too late means running out and losing sales. Ordering too much means
paying to store things — and some stock can spoil or go out of date. How MUCH
to order each time is a separate decision from WHEN to order.

An analogy: the reorder point is like your car's fuel light. It comes on early
enough to reach a gas station. But the analogy stops there — a fuel light is set
once by the carmaker, while a reorder point must be **reviewed regularly**,
because it relies on the past predicting the future. A promotion, a new
customer, or a supply problem can make yesterday's numbers wrong.

### Check yourself
1. What sets the reorder point? *(Daily use multiplied by delivery days, plus
   safety stock — all three parts, per the source formula.)*
2. What is safety stock for? *(Demand spikes and late deliveries.)*
3. Why review reorder points regularly? *(They assume the past predicts the
   future; promotions, new customers, or disruptions break that assumption.)*

### Fidelity note (part of the check)
Preserved: the point/quantity distinction, the variability rule, both failure
costs, and the review caveat. No fixed numbers were invented; the bakery example
illustrates the formula in the source.

# Topic: household budgeting (self-study variation)

## SOURCE (give this to the assistant)

A household budget is a plan that allocates expected income to expected
expenses over a period, usually a month. Expenses are commonly split into
fixed costs, which stay the same each period (rent, insurance, loan
payments), and variable costs, which change with usage or choices
(groceries, fuel, entertainment). A budget is balanced when planned expenses
plus planned savings do not exceed expected income. Savings set aside for
irregular but predictable expenses — annual insurance premiums, car
maintenance, holiday gifts — are called sinking funds; without them, these
expenses appear as surprises even though they are foreseeable. An emergency
fund is different: it covers genuinely unpredictable events such as job loss
or urgent repairs, and a common guideline is three to six months of
essential expenses. Guidelines such as allocating 50% of income to needs,
30% to wants, and 20% to savings are starting points, not rules; households
with high fixed costs or irregular income must adapt the ratios. A budget
based on estimated numbers drifts from reality, so spending should be
reviewed against the plan regularly, and the plan revised when income or
circumstances change.

## SAMPLE OUTPUT (what a good result looks like)

### The main idea
A budget is a plan made **before** the money is spent: you decide where your
income should go each month, instead of finding out afterwards where it went.

### Two kinds of spending
Some costs are the same every month — rent, insurance, loan payments. These
are called **fixed costs**. Other costs change depending on what you do —
food, fuel, fun. These are **variable costs**. A budget lists both and adds
planned savings. The plan works when all of it together is not more than the
money coming in.

### Saving for things you can see coming
Some expenses do not happen every month but are not surprises either: a
yearly insurance bill, car repairs, holiday gifts. Money set aside a little
at a time for these is called a **sinking fund**. Without one, a bill you
could have predicted feels like an emergency.

### Saving for things you cannot see coming
A real **emergency fund** is for events you cannot predict — losing a job,
an urgent repair. A common guideline is enough to cover three to six months
of essential costs. Guideline, not rule: the same is true of the well-known
50/30/20 split (needs/wants/savings). If your rent is high or your income
changes month to month, your numbers will look different — and that is fine.

An analogy: a budget is like a shopping list. You write it before entering
the store, so the store does not decide for you. But the analogy stops
there — a shopping list is finished after one trip, while a budget must be
**checked and revised regularly**, because it is built on estimates that
drift away from real life.

### Check yourself
1. What is the difference between fixed and variable costs? *(Fixed stay the
   same each period, like rent; variable change with usage or choices, like
   groceries.)*
2. What is a sinking fund for? *(Irregular but predictable expenses —
   foreseeable bills that would otherwise feel like surprises.)*
3. Is the 50/30/20 split a rule? *(No — a starting point; households with
   high fixed costs or irregular income must adapt the ratios.)*

### Fidelity note (part of the check)
Preserved: the fixed/variable distinction, the sinking-fund vs
emergency-fund distinction, the "guideline not rule" caveat on both the
three-to-six-months figure and the 50/30/20 split, and the review caveat.
No numbers were invented beyond those in the source.

# Topic: the water cycle (self-study variation)

## SOURCE (give this to the assistant)

The water cycle describes the continuous movement of water on, above, and below
Earth's surface. Solar energy drives evaporation from oceans, lakes, and soil;
plants release additional water vapor through transpiration. As moist air rises
and cools, vapor condenses into droplets, forming clouds. When droplets grow
heavy enough they fall as precipitation — rain or snow depending on temperature.
Precipitation either runs off into rivers and eventually the ocean, soaks into
the ground to recharge groundwater, or is stored temporarily as ice and snow.
Residence times vary enormously: water may stay in the atmosphere about nine
days on average, but in glaciers or deep aquifers for centuries or longer. The
cycle conserves total water: it changes form and location but is neither created
nor destroyed in the process.

## SAMPLE OUTPUT (what a good result looks like)

### The main idea
Earth keeps reusing the same water, moving it in a loop between the sea, the
sky, and the land.

### How the loop works
The sun warms water in oceans and lakes and turns some of it into **water
vapor** — water in the form of a gas. Plants add vapor to the air too. High in
the sky, the vapor cools and turns back into tiny droplets that make clouds.
When droplets get heavy, they fall as rain — or snow, when it is cold. That
water then flows to rivers and the sea, soaks into the ground, or is stored as
ice, and the loop begins again.

### The part people miss
Water does not move through the loop at one speed. A drop may spend about nine
days in the air — but centuries locked in a glacier or deep underground.

An analogy: the cycle is like a giant recycling system — nothing is thrown
away, everything is reused. The analogy stops here: real recycling changes
products into new products, while the water cycle keeps the water itself the
same and only changes its **form** (liquid, vapor, ice) and its **place**.

### Check yourself
1. What powers the water cycle? *(The sun's energy.)*
2. Name the three places rain can go after it falls. *(Rivers/sea, into the
   ground, stored as ice or snow.)*
3. Is new water created in the cycle? *(No — the same water changes form and
   place.)*

### Fidelity note (part of the check)
Preserved: transpiration (as "plants add vapor"), the residence-time contrast,
and conservation of water. Simplification flagged in review: "about nine days"
is an average, not a rule — the word "may" keeps that honest.
